claims.text: The as-synthesized multi-element nanoparticles have a near-equiatomic composition.
The as-synthesized nanoparticles are single-phase random solid solutions.
Atomic-size mismatch creates atomic-scale lattice strain fields in near-equiatomic nanoparticles.
High configurational entropy and lattice strain kinetically impede atomic diffusion.
Impeded atomic diffusion suppresses elemental segregation and phase separation at elevated temperatures.
Nanoparticles with greater atomic-size mismatch have greater lattice strain than nanoparticles with minimal atomic-size mismatch.
Nanoparticles with minimal atomic-size mismatch permit easier atomic diffusion.
Easier atomic diffusion causes an earlier onset of phase instability.
Under high-temperature exposure, nanoparticles with greater atomic-size mismatch will retain a single-phase structure better than nanoparticles with minimal mismatch.
Under high-temperature exposure, nanoparticles with greater atomic-size mismatch will retain a more uniform elemental distribution than nanoparticles with minimal mismatch.
Nanoparticles with minimal atomic-size mismatch have lower resistance to thermally induced segregation.
The proposed kinetic stabilization applies only below the thermodynamic stability limit of the solid solution.
Moderately favorable mixing enthalpy is a boundary condition for the proposed stabilization mechanism.
Extreme temperatures or strongly unfavorable elemental interactions can override kinetic stabilization by lattice strain and configurational entropy.
The atomic-size-mismatch threshold required for significant stabilization is unknown.
The temperature limits of the proposed stabilization mechanism are unknown.
